title: Madisonville, a courthouse town on McGary and Silkwood land
summary: Hopkins County was created on December 9, 1806, and in 1807 its seat was laid out on 40 acres given by Daniel McGary and Solomon Silkwood and named for Secretary of State James Madison.
bodyMarkdown:
Madisonville began with a gift of forty acres and a name borrowed from Thomas Jefferson's cabinet. The Kentucky legislature [created Hopkins County on December 9, 1806](https://grokipedia.com/page/Madisonville,_Kentucky), cutting it from Henderson County, and within a year the new county had a seat of justice.

## A general's county

The county took its name from [Samuel Hopkins](/people/#samuel-hopkins), who had [served on Washington's staff](https://history.ky.gov/markers/county-named-1806-521) and in many campaigns of the Revolution. He came to Kentucky in 1797 as agent for the Transylvania Company, the land company behind the town of [Henderson](/stories/henderson-at-red-banks/) at the Red Banks.

In 1799 he was named judge of the first court held in the original Henderson County, which then took in this whole district. He later sat in both houses of the legislature, commanded on the western frontier in 1812 and served in Congress from 1813 to 1815.

Many of the district's settlers were newcomers on military land. Some of the [first families were Revolutionary War veterans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkins_County,_Kentucky) holding Virginia land grants southwest of the Green River. One of the grantees was [Baron von Steuben](https://grokipedia.com/page/Friedrich_Wilhelm_von_Steuben), the Prussian drillmaster of Washington's army; a state marker says he came to [inspect his military grants and visited the lick](https://history.ky.gov/markers/steubens-lick) that still carries his name north of town. Early roads followed animal trails to the salt and mineral springs, and the main traces ran from the county seat to Henderson, Hopkinsville and Russellville.

## Forty acres on Main Street

In 1807, [one year after the county was established](https://history.ky.gov/markers/madisonville), the seat was laid out on 40 acres given by Daniel McGary and Solomon Silkwood. Between them the two men [held about 1,000 acres](https://grokipedia.com/page/Madisonville,_Kentucky) along what became Main Street, and a plain courthouse went up that same year. The town was named for [James Madison](/people/#james-madison), who was [then Secretary of State](https://grokipedia.com/page/James_Madison) under Jefferson, and it was incorporated in 1810.

For most of the 1800s Madisonville was a farm town, and tobacco was the leading crop of the county.

## War on the courthouse square

The Civil War split Hopkins County. In 1862, the [state marker at Arch and Spring Streets](https://history.ky.gov/markers/army-of-six) says, 300 Union troops sent to burn the homes of Confederate sympathizers withdrew after Adam Johnson bluffed them with six men. Captain L. D. Hockersmith of Morgan's cavalry, who [helped dig the tunnel](https://history.ky.gov/markers/the-hockersmith-house) by which John Hunt Morgan escaped the Ohio penitentiary on November 27, 1863, lived on South Scott Street.

On December 17, 1864, Gen. Hylan B. Lyon's raiders [burned the courthouse](https://history.ky.gov/markers/courthouse-burned-255), which Union forces had been using. The county records were saved.

## Coal and rails

Around 1837 a blacksmith named James Woolfolk found [coal cropping out on his land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkins_County,_Kentucky). John Bayless Earle opened the county's first mine in 1869, and the next year the Louisville & Nashville Railroad built south from Henderson through Madisonville toward Nashville, turning mining into the county's great industry. By the early 1900s Madisonville was a [rail hub, a coal center and a large tobacco market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madisonville,_Kentucky).

## Kentucky today

Madisonville is still the Hopkins County seat, and Main Street still runs over the McGary and Silkwood ground. The courthouse lawn carries the marker for Samuel Hopkins and the marker for the 1864 burning. The town also claims Maurice K. Gordon, who [gave the American Legion its name](https://history.ky.gov/markers/madisonville) at its founding in Paris in March 1919. The map pin marks the courthouse lawn.
